title: Solution Design & Architecture
intro: Solution Design & Architecture is the domain where the exam tests whether you can turn a messy business situation into a well-shaped Claude system: deciding what the model should and should not do, choosing the simplest pattern that meets the requirement, and defending every design choice against cost, latency, reliability, and business-value constraints. Nearly every question is a scenario in which several designs would technically work and you must pick the one that best fits the stated constraints. Expect to reason with Anthropic's building-effective-agents taxonomy — augmented LLM, workflow patterns, and agents — and to justify architecture in terms of measurable business outcomes rather than technical elegance.

objectives.objective: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
objectives.explanation:
Translation is the discipline of converting a stakeholder's problem statement — often vague ('support costs are too high') or solution-shaped ('build us an agent') — into a precise definition of what work exists, which parts of it are genuinely language problems, and what a successful outcome would measurably look like. The first move is decomposing the business process into subtasks and sorting them into two piles: subtasks that involve understanding or producing natural language and tolerating ambiguity, which are candidates for Claude, and subtasks that are rule evaluation, arithmetic, lookups, or fixed transformations, which belong in deterministic code. A model applied to a rules problem is slower, costlier, and less reliable than the code that solves it exactly; code applied to a language problem simply fails.

The second move is establishing success criteria and a baseline before any architecture is discussed. Without a measured baseline (current cost per document, current handle time, current error rate) and a target, no design can be evaluated, no pilot can prove value, and pattern debates become unresolvable matters of taste. Architects who let teams argue workflow-versus-agent before anyone defines 'good' are letting the least important decision go first.

The third move is scoping. Large visions ('handle everything customers ask') should be cut down to an MVP slice chosen for high volume, objectively checkable outcomes, and contained blast radius — not for being the most impressive demo. The narrow slice builds the team's evaluation and guardrail muscle, proves value in numbers executives trust, and creates the platform for expansion. Finally, treat stakeholder solution language as a requirement to be recovered, not obeyed: when an executive asks for 'an autonomous agent' to run a fixed monthly report, the underlying requirement is a reliable report, and the honest translation may involve very little model at all.
objectives.whyItMatters: Most failed LLM initiatives fail here, before any code is written: a model is pointed at a deterministic problem, success is never defined so the pilot cannot prove anything, or scope sprawls until nothing ships. The translation step determines whether everything downstream — pattern choice, evaluation, cost model — has a foundation. In production, systems built on a bad translation exhibit the most expensive failure mode there is: they work as designed while solving the wrong problem.

examples.title: Insurance claims: splitting the pipeline correctly
examples.body: A carrier wants Claude across its whole claims pipeline: reading adjuster notes, extracting loss details, applying coverage rules, calculating payouts. The architect maps the subtasks. Reading free-text notes and emails is a language problem with irreducible ambiguity — a strong Claude fit. Coverage rules and payout formulas have exact, auditable answers — putting them in a prompt would trade correctness for nothing. The resulting design uses Claude for extraction and summarization, emits a structured record, and hands it to deterministic rules code for adjudication and math. Each half is now testable with the right method: evals for the model stage, unit tests for the rules.

examples.title: The vague cost complaint
examples.body: A SaaS company says only that support costs are too high. Instead of proposing an assistant, the architect segments the ticket data: 40% are password resets and billing lookups that existing self-service already answers, 35% are how-to questions answerable from documentation, 25% are ambiguous multi-system escalations. The translation maps each segment to its cheapest adequate mechanism — routing and discoverability fixes for the first, a retrieval-augmented Claude answerer with measurable deflection for the second, and no automation (yet) for the hardest third. The proposal now has a baseline, a target metric, and a defensible scope.

pitfalls: Accepting the stakeholder's solution language ('we need an agent') as the requirement — the requirement is the outcome, and the honest design may need far less autonomy than requested.

Running rules, thresholds, or arithmetic through the model because a uniform stack feels cleaner; deterministic logic in a prompt is strictly worse on accuracy, cost, and auditability than the same logic in code.
Choosing an architecture before success criteria and a baseline exist, which makes every later evaluation an argument about opinions instead of numbers.
Scoping the MVP by what demos best rather than by volume, measurability, and contained blast radius — impressive-but-unmeasurable pilots cannot prove value.
Assuming a big-bang launch across all use cases gathers data faster; it actually spreads evaluation and hardening effort so thin that no use case gets production-grade.

objectives.objective: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
objectives.explanation:
An end-to-end Claude architecture has four stages, and each exists to catch a class of failure the others cannot. The input stage validates and normalizes what enters the model: quality gates on OCR output, schema checks on structured fields, classification and routing of raw requests. The rule is garbage in, garbage out — no downstream model tier can recover information that never arrived, so defects that originate in capture or preprocessing must be fixed or rejected there, not compensated for later.

The processing stage is where the model (or chain of model calls) does its work, and the output stage is where its results are checked before they touch anything real. Output validation should be deterministic wherever a ground truth exists: a suggested billing code is checked against the licensed code list, a JSON payload against a schema, a computed field against its source. Where no mechanical oracle exists — subtle transcription errors, judgment calls — the control is targeted human review, routed by model confidence and by sampling. A model output should never write into a system of record without passing through whichever of these gates its risk demands.

Humans sit in the flow as a scarce resource positioned by risk, not applied uniformly. High-impact, irreversible actions (moving money, changing medical records) get a pre-execution approval gate; low-risk, high-volume actions flow through with post-hoc sampled review. Reviewing everything recreates the manual workload and destroys the value case; reviewing nothing fails accountability requirements.

The feedback stage is the one teams most often omit. Every human correction, edit, and escalation is a free labeled example. A complete architecture captures that signal, mines it for systematic failure patterns, feeds fixes back into prompts, few-shot examples, and retrieval configuration, and keeps the accumulated cases as a regression eval. A pipeline without this loop is static by construction: it will make the same mistakes at month twelve that it made at month one.
objectives.whyItMatters: Production incidents in LLM systems overwhelmingly happen at the boundaries — bad input the model gamely processed, plausible output nobody validated, human review placed where it adds friction instead of safety — and stagnation happens when correction signal is thrown away. Architects who design all four stages deliberately ship systems that fail safely and improve over time; those who design only the processing stage ship a demo with production traffic.

examples.title: Billing codes that do not exist
examples.body: A revenue-cycle system has Claude suggest ICD-10 codes that flow straight into billing, and auditors find well-formed but nonexistent codes. The tempting fixes are all probabilistic: a stronger model, more few-shot examples, a self-verification pass. The architectural fix is a deterministic output-validation stage — every suggested code is checked against the licensed code list before it reaches billing. The invalid-code error class drops to zero at negligible cost, because where a ground-truth reference exists, validation belongs in code at the output boundary, not in the model's judgment.

examples.title: The support desk that never improved
examples.body: Agents edit Claude-drafted replies before sending, fixing the same mistakes for six months while edit rates stay flat at 45%. The pipeline runs input, retrieval, generation, human edit — and discards the edits. The missing stage is feedback capture: log each draft alongside its human-corrected version, cluster the diffs to find systematic failures (stale retrieval sources, missing product knowledge, tone errors), fix the top clusters in prompts and retrieval, and keep the corrected pairs as a regression suite. Within a quarter the edit rate finally moves, because the system is now consuming the supervision signal it always produced.

pitfalls: Compensating for bad input with a bigger model — no model tier reconstructs data that was garbled or lost upstream, so quality gates belong before the processing stage.
Validating model output with another model when a deterministic check exists; a lookup or schema check is certain and nearly free, while a second model pass is probabilistic and costs money.

Placing human review uniformly over everything (destroying the efficiency case) or only at intake (leaving the actual risky action ungated) instead of at high-impact, irreversible actions in proportion to risk.
Treating human edits and corrections as terminal byproducts rather than capturing them as labeled data that drives prompt updates and regression evals.
Confusing structured output (valid JSON, filled fields) with correct output — a schema constrains shape, not truth, so structural checks never replace content validation.

objectives.objective: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
objectives.explanation:
Anthropic's taxonomy for building effective agents is an escalation ladder, and the governing rule is to use the simplest pattern that meets the requirement. The first rung is the augmented LLM: a single model call enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory. A surprising share of production tasks — single-turn question answering over indexed data, classification, extraction, drafting — resolve here, with flat predictable cost and the shortest path to launch.

The second rung is workflows: systems where your code orchestrates predefined model calls. The named patterns each answer a specific structural problem. Prompt chaining fits tasks with fixed, ordered, individually checkable steps, with programmatic gates between them. Routing fits inputs that fall into distinct categories needing different prompts, tools, or handling — its signature symptom is one general prompt where improving one category degrades another. Parallelization comes in two forms: sectioning, which splits a large input into independent parts processed simultaneously, and voting, which runs the same task multiple times and aggregates for confidence. Orchestrator-workers has a model dynamically decide which subtasks a given input needs and delegate to workers. Evaluator-optimizer loops a generator against a critic and fits when evaluation criteria are articulable and iteration demonstrably improves output.

The third rung is agents: the model directs its own tool use in a loop, deciding each next step from what it just observed. Agency is justified only when the solution path cannot be predicted in advance — open-ended investigation, debugging, research — because autonomy buys flexibility at the price of higher cost, variable latency, and a larger error surface. The selection question is always empirical: are the steps knowable at design time? If yes, a workflow under code control is more predictable, testable, and cheap. Constraints can also override quality preferences — a hard 2-second SLA rules out an open-ended agent loop regardless of how good its answers are, because patterns with unbounded call structures cannot be engineered to a fixed latency.
objectives.whyItMatters: Pattern choice sets the cost, latency, reliability, and debuggability envelope of the entire system before a single prompt is written. Teams that reach for agents by default ship systems that are expensive, slow, and hard to test for tasks a three-call workflow would have handled; teams that under-power genuinely open-ended tasks ship rigid playbooks that fail on every case the designers did not foresee. The exam repeatedly tests whether you can read a scenario's constraints and place it on the right rung.

examples.title: Compliance narratives: fixed steps mean a workflow
examples.body: A fintech processes suspicious-activity narratives through three invariant steps — extract entities, classify typology against a fixed list, draft a regulator summary — with quality checks per step and a requirement for consistent, explainable processing. Every signal points to prompt chaining: the steps are known at design time, ordered, and individually checkable, so code invokes each call in sequence with programmatic gates between them. An agent could do this, but there is nothing for it to decide, so its nondeterminism, latency, and cost would be pure loss in a compliance setting.

examples.title: Incident investigation: unpredictable steps mean an agent
examples.body: A hospital wants Claude to investigate integration incidents where lab results fail to reach patient charts. Root causes range across interface engines, mapping mismatches, vendor outages, and expired credentials, and each finding changes what to examine next — the diagnostic path cannot be enumerated per symptom. This is the profile that earns agency: the model queries logs, configs, and monitoring through read-only tools, forms hypotheses, and tests them iteratively. Read-only access bounds the blast radius, and the hours of engineer time saved per incident absorb the agent's cost and latency.

pitfalls: Defaulting to an agent because it is the most capable pattern — if the steps are predictable, an agent adds cost, latency, and nondeterminism while removing testability.
Cramming multiple distinct steps into one monolithic prompt when intermediate checkpoints matter, sacrificing the per-step gates and traceability that chaining provides.
Running specialized prompts in parallel on every input to avoid building a router — parallelization aggregates diverse work; category dispatch is routing's job and a cheap classifier does it.
Ignoring hard latency or cost constraints when selecting a pattern; an SLA measured at p95 rules out unbounded agent loops no matter how good their output is.
Using evaluator-optimizer without articulable evaluation criteria — a critic with nothing concrete to check against adds cost per request without a reliable quality gain.

objectives.objective: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
objectives.explanation:
The first multi-agent design decision is whether to be multi-agent at all. A single agent with well-designed tools beats a multi-agent system whenever each request needs a bounded, predictable slice of capability: no coordination overhead, no context duplication, one system to evaluate and debug. Decomposing agents along org-chart or data-source lines ('one agent per system') is the most common over-engineering pattern in this space — the boundaries people reflexively draw for teams of humans are usually just tool boundaries for one agent. Multi-agent designs earn their cost when breadth and parallelism are the bottleneck: work that exceeds one context window, many independent subtasks against a deadline, or subtask sets that vary per input.

The dominant orchestration shape is orchestrator-workers: a lead process (or lead agent) decomposes the job, dispatches workers, and owns synthesis. Use a fixed dispatch when the subtasks are static; use a model-driven orchestrator when the needed subtasks only become clear on inspecting each input. Peer patterns — agents passing work among themselves without a lead — suit debate and negotiation-style tasks but have no owner of the plan or of termination, so they fit poorly for coverage-style work.

Context management is the central axis. The default for parallel work is isolation: each worker receives only its own subtask brief and the minimal context it needs, and coordination happens through explicit interfaces defined up front, not through a shared mutable conversation. Shared context causes both quality failures (agents acting on each other's stale plans, overwriting each other's work) and cost failures (every worker re-reads the whole history on every call). Cost multiplies with agent count times context size, so the two levers are minimal isolated contexts and model tiering by role — cheap fast models like Haiku for narrow high-volume worker tasks, a stronger model reserved for the orchestrator's planning and synthesis.

Finally, design for worker failure. A subagent hitting a bad feed or an API outage should fail alone: the orchestrator collects successful results, retries or flags the failed subtask, and degrades to a partial result with explicit gaps rather than aborting the run. All-or-nothing orchestration turns any single worker's bad night into a system-wide outage.
objectives.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems multiply everything — capability, but also token cost, latency, failure modes, and debugging surface. In production, the difference between a multi-agent system that ships and one that gets rolled back is almost always discipline on these fundamentals: agents only where parallel breadth demands them, contexts isolated and minimal, models tiered by role, and failures contained at the orchestrator instead of propagated.

examples.title: Due diligence under a 48-hour clock
examples.body: A private-equity firm must research dozens of independent questions across a large document room within 48 hours; a single agent has the quality but not the throughput, and its context fills before the question list ends. This is the canonical orchestrator-workers case: an orchestrator spawns a worker per question, each with an isolated context sized to that one question, workers run in parallel to beat the deadline, and the orchestrator alone assembles the synthesis. Isolation is what makes the parallelism clean — no worker pays tokens for, or gets confused by, the other workers' material.

examples.title: Five agents that should have been five tools
examples.body: A platform team proposes five specialist agents — logs, metrics, deployments, tickets, docs — behind a router agent, for a workload of engineer questions that each touch one or two sources. The review conclusion: one agent, five well-designed tools. The specialist split guarantees handoffs, duplicated context, and multiplied cost on every question while adding no capability, because per-source competence lives in tool design, not in agent separation. Multi-agent structure is justified by scale and parallelism, and this workload has neither.

pitfalls: Splitting into multiple agents along data-source or org-chart lines when a single agent with good tools handles the bounded workload cheaper and more debuggably.
Sharing one running conversation among parallel agents 'so everyone stays informed' — shared mutable context causes stale-plan collisions and multiplies token spend by agent count.
Running all agents on the most capable model by default; worker subtasks are usually narrow enough for Haiku, and uniform Opus turns the cost multiplication into a budget crisis.
Building all-or-nothing orchestration where one worker's failure aborts the run — the orchestrator should contain failures, retry selectively, and deliver partial results with explicit gaps.
Using peer patterns for coverage work; without a lead there is no owner of the plan, no deduplication of effort, and no deterministic termination.

objectives.objective: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
objectives.explanation:
Decomposition turns a task too large, too opaque, or too unreliable for one model call into stages that can each be gated, tested, and debugged. The first principle is to cut along natural boundaries. Documents have structural seams (sections, clauses, schedules); processes have stage seams (generate, then check, then translate; extract facts, then adjudicate). Cutting at these seams keeps each unit semantically whole and gives every checklist item or validation an obvious home. Arbitrary cuts — fixed-size windows through a contract, per-file review of a cross-file change — sever exactly the relationships the task depends on.

Choose the decomposition shape by the problem's structure. Sequential dependency calls for chaining: stage B consumes stage A's output, with a programmatic gate between them so defects stop propagating (non-compliant copy never reaches the translation stage). Independent parts of a large input call for sectioning: parallel processing with an aggregation step, which also attacks latency. Unreliable judgment on a hard task calls for voting: multiple independent attempts at the same task, aggregated by a rule matched to the cost asymmetry — union the findings when misses are expensive, majority when false positives are. One especially valuable seam is perception versus judgment: separating 'produce a structured record of the facts' from 'reason over that record' creates a validated intermediate artifact, makes each error class attributable, and gives auditors a decision trace.

The counterweight is over-decomposition. Every added boundary costs latency, tokens, and a new failure opportunity, and long chains abort on any step's failure. A boundary must earn its place with measurable quality, reliability, or checkability gains; a twelve-step chain that matches a three-step prototype's quality is nine steps of pure cost. The test is empirical — compare against a simpler baseline — and the corrective is consolidation back to the simplest structure that meets the requirement.
objectives.whyItMatters: Decomposition is how architects convert 'the model is unreliable on this big task' into a set of small tasks the model is reliable on, and how opaque end-to-end failures become attributable to a stage someone can fix. Done well it is also the cost and latency lever: parallel sections beat sequential passes, and validated intermediates prevent expensive downstream rework. Done badly — wrong seams or too many of them — it produces fragile chains that are slower and no better than a single good prompt.

examples.title: 300-page credit agreements in under an hour
examples.body: Whole-document review misses issues buried mid-agreement, and reviews must finish within an hour. The agreements have strong conventional structure — definitions, covenants, events of default, schedules — so the architect sections along those boundaries, reviews each section in parallel against only the checklist items relevant to it, and aggregates findings with cross-reference handling. Each unit stays semantically whole, attention stays local, and parallelism meets the deadline. Fixed 20-page windows would have hit the latency target too, but at the price of covenants reviewed in severed fragments.

examples.title: Vulnerability review where misses are expensive
examples.body: A single PR-review call flags issues inconsistently, and a missed injection flaw costs far more than triaging extra false positives. The right decomposition is voting: several independent review passes over the same diff, optionally with varied prompts, with findings unioned so anything any pass catches gets triaged. The aggregation rule follows the cost asymmetry — union maximizes recall where misses dominate the cost. Sectioning by file would not help, because the problem is variance in what one pass notices, not the size of the input.

pitfalls: Chunking by fixed size when the artifact has natural structural boundaries — arbitrary cuts sever clauses and cross-references that section-aligned cuts preserve.

Confusing sectioning with voting: sectioning covers a large input by splitting it; voting builds confidence on a hard judgment by repeating it — applying one where the other is needed leaves the actual problem untouched.
Adding chain steps without measuring their contribution; every boundary costs latency and failure surface, and steps that do not move quality metrics should be merged away.
Fusing perception and judgment in one call, which makes extraction errors and reasoning errors indistinguishable and leaves nothing validatable in between.
Letting one early model call decide what the later calls examine without any recall safeguard, creating a single point of failure at the top of the chain.

objectives.objective: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
objectives.explanation:
Every Claude architecture should be able to answer one question in business language: which value pillar does this serve, and what metric will prove it? The pillars are distinct and the distinctions matter. Efficiency is the same defined work done cheaper or faster — unit cost and cycle time are its metrics. Productivity is people accomplishing more or higher-value output — throughput per person, or hours redirected to higher-value work. Transformation is a genuinely new capability, offering, or revenue stream that the prior operating model could not produce — measured in new revenue and capability, not in cost per unit. Cost is hitting an explicit spend target, and performance means meeting defined SLAs and service commitments. Misnaming the pillar is not cosmetic: it sets the wrong metrics in front of executives, funds the initiative from the wrong case, and mismeasures success afterward.

Pillars operate as design inputs, not post-hoc labels. A contracted p95 latency bound is a binding constraint that drives model choice and pattern choice — it can rule out an agent loop or a heavyweight model regardless of output quality, because patterns with unbounded call structures cannot be engineered to a fixed latency. A mandated cost ceiling drives model tiering, routing by request difficulty, and retrieval instead of context stuffing; the architectural discipline is to remove spend that buys no quality before asking the business to move the target.

The pillar framework is also the architect's defense against technology-led initiatives. A proposal that cannot name its target process, owner, baseline, and metric — 'we need a flagship AI initiative,' 'competitors are doing agents' — is not ready to be designed, and the architect's correct move is to require or facilitate that discovery before any architecture work begins. Instrumenting an aimless system just measures aimlessness precisely; the value case precedes the solution.
objectives.whyItMatters: Architecture decisions are ultimately funding decisions, and systems that cannot articulate their value pillar get built on enthusiasm and cancelled on budget review. In production, the pillar determines real engineering choices — which model tier, which pattern, where the latency budget goes — and an SLA breach or a blown unit-cost target is a business failure regardless of how good the outputs are. Architects who tie designs to measurable value ship systems that survive scrutiny.

examples.title: Engineering to a 3-second contract
examples.body: A telehealth platform must answer routine pre-visit questions at p95 under 3 seconds, with financial penalties for breaches. The team's favorite design — Opus with a rich multi-step retrieval flow — produces excellent answers in 6 to 9 seconds. The SLA is a binding input, so the architect reworks the design around it: a faster model, a single-pass retrieval flow with bounded call structure, quality-checked against the contract's scope of routine questions. Patient testing confirming a preference for fast answers corroborates the call, but the deciding factor is that a contracted metric is engineered to, not negotiated away or masked with a progress spinner.

examples.title: Hitting a $0.15 ticket ceiling
examples.body: Support responses cost $0.42 per ticket against a $0.15 mandate, with 70% of tickets simple and every ticket getting the same Sonnet pipeline with the full knowledge base stuffed into context. The architecture has obvious waste, so the cost pillar directs specific levers: route the simple 70% to Haiku, retrieve only relevant knowledge-base sections per ticket instead of paying for everything on every request, and reserve Sonnet for the complex 30%. The ceiling is met by removing spend that bought no quality — tiering and retrieval scope — before any conversation about relaxing the target or lowering the quality floor.

pitfalls: Labeling any AI deployment 'transformation' — if the workflow, outputs, and volumes are unchanged and the gain is cheaper-faster, it is efficiency, and inflating the claim distorts the metrics executives track.
Treating a contracted SLA as negotiable output of the design rather than a binding input that constrains model and pattern choice from the start.
Approving initiatives with no named process, owner, baseline, or metric on the theory that benefits can be discovered after launch — instrumentation cannot rescue an aimless system.

Meeting cost targets by uniform downgrades (everything to the cheapest model) instead of matching model tier and context size to each request's actual needs, which sacrifices quality where it was genuinely required.
Justifying scope by competitor behavior — another company's agent deployments cannot supply your value case, because their baselines and economics are theirs.
